newsitem.title: USA: US corporate debt issuance at record pace - PSA.
newsitem.headline: US corporate debt issuance at record pace - PSA.

text.p: Anticipation of higher borrowing rates by U.S. corporate debt issuers led to a record-setting pace of new supply in the first quarter on 1997, according to PSA The Bond Market Trade Association.

Issuance in corporate bonds for Q1 1997 hit $138.3 billion compared with $104.6 billion sold in the same time frame last year, a jump of 32.3 percent, PSA said. At that rate, issuance could top $500 billion for the year and handily break the record of $427.1 billion set in 1996, it added.

Factors behind the increase included heavy investor demand, continued capital requirements of corporations and a "rush-to-market" by issuers anticipating interest rate hikes by the (Federal Reserve), said PSA.
Investment grade volume rose 31.5 percent in the quarter to $116.6 billion. High-yield issuance rose 36.5 percent to $21.7 billion.

Fixed-rate capital securities, which are treated as subordinated junior debt with tax-deductable payments by the issuer, accounted for a significant portion of that rise, PSA said. An estimated $15 billion of the securities were sold in the first three months of the year, more than four times that seen in Q1 1996.
PSA noted the Clinton Administration has questioned the deductability of capital securities in recent budget proposals and future volume is uncertain.

Issuance from all fixed-income markets grew 11.1 percent, largely due to a 24.3 percent surge in the volume of U.S. Federal Agency debt in addition to the increase in corporates, PSA said. Asset-backeds, meanwhile, first quarter volume fell marginally to $33.4 billion from $33.9 billion in Q1 1996.
The PSA report was based on data from Securities Data Company.
